title: Auditing Question-Order Effects in Large Language Models with the QQ Equality: Mechanism Characterization and a Saturation Caveat
abstract: Human survey respondents exhibit question-order effects that satisfy the QQ (quantum question) equality, an a priori, parameter-free prediction of the projective quantum question-order model. We develop the QQ equality into an audit criterion for sequential judgments of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Theoretically, we characterize which mechanism classes satisfy it robustly: marginal-independent kernels satisfy QQ iff all four mismatch transition rates coincide (a class containing the 2D rank-1 projective model with a fixed measurement pair under state variation); a polarity- and position-dependent repetition family is characterized by an exact cross-symmetry condition with closed-form violations; QQ-satisfying behaviors are closed under order-matched mixing; and the rank-2 Contextuality-by-Default criterion translates into audit coordinates as $|\qQQ|\le\OSS$, where $\OSS$ (the order-sensitivity score) totals the order sensitivity of the two marginals. Methodologically, we develop a pre-specified, audit-logged pipeline applicable to any model exposing next-token log-probabilities; it combines worst-case robustness envelopes, sampling-consistency spot checks, full label counterbalancing, and a saturation diagnostic. Empirically, in a first-signal pilot on an open-weight instruction-tuned model under two framings, all pre-specified health gates passed, yet 17/18 and 7/8 item pairs, respectively, were saturated (near-deterministic), and no item was certified residually contextual. Forced-binary next-token log-probabilities were thus inadequate for distribution-level QQ audits under the tested model and prompting conditions; we recommend pre-specified saturation diagnostics whenever next-token distributions are treated as survey-response distributions.
summary: This work adapts the QQ equality, originally from human survey data, into a rigorous audit tool to test question-order effects in LLMs. The methodology combines theoretical characterization of contextuality with an empirical pipeline that must account for response saturation. Ultimately, it highlights the limitations of using simple next-token probabilities when modeling complex distributional phenomena.
main_problem: The paper audits whether the sequential judgment behavior of autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) satisfies the QQ (quantum question) equality, a constraint derived from human survey data.
main_result: Empirical testing showed that while standard health gates passed, the LLM responses were saturated (near-deterministic), indicating that forced-binary next-token probabilities are inadequate for robust distribution-level audits.
method: The authors developed a pre-specified, audit-logged pipeline combining worst-case robustness envelopes, sampling checks, and crucially, a saturation diagnostic to test the QQ equality.
model_or_system: The system under study is an autoregressive LLM whose next-token log-probabilities are treated as synthetic survey response distributions. The theoretical framework draws parallels with projective quantum measurement models.
key_observables: The primary observable is the $	ext{qQQ}$ equality, which quantifies question-order effects (QOE) in sequential judgments; contextuality is assessed via the CbD criterion ($\Gamma$).
important_parameters: Saturation threshold (e.g., $>0.99$ probability), and the specific structure of the LLM's next-token log-probabilities.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is treating LLM next-token probabilities as genuine survey response distributions, which requires a saturation diagnostic to validate.
figures_summary: Not specified in detail, but the notes reference tables summarizing 18 frozen question pairs and their mapping/set types.
paper_structure: The paper moves from establishing the theoretical basis of the QQ equality derived from human data, through characterizing mechanism classes that satisfy it (e.g., marginal-independent kernels), to developing a rigorous audit pipeline, and concluding with an empirical pilot demonstrating diagnostic limitations.
why_interesting: It provides a novel, physics-inspired statistical framework for auditing complex AI models by mapping their sequential decision-making process onto concepts from quantum information theory (contextuality/order effects).
